drive_physically: Charge-balanced current pulses across an electrode–tissue interface, Faradaic and non-Faradaic charge transfer [63]
proposed_primary_coupling: Axonal excitation; driving term is the second spatial derivative of extracellular potential along the fibre (computational) [33]; axons before somata, polarity- and orientation-dependent [34]
named_rival: Informational lesion: high-frequency stimulation makes output regular and variance-free, so the nucleus fires but stops transmitting information (computational) [133]
dose_quantities_reported: Amplitude, pulse width, frequency, train timing; safety bounded jointly by charge density and charge per phase, ~10–800 µC/cm² and 0.05–5 µC/phase, cat cortex [16], fitted as a log-linear limit [17]; effective dose often omitted [2]
resolution_reported: Effective spatial unit is the connected fibre set: structural and functional connectivity independently predicted motor gain in 51 patients and replicated in a second cohort [132]; chronaxie ~50–100 µs for central myelinated axons, 200–700 µs in grey matter [34]
dominant_evidence_base: Human clinical cohorts [132]; cat cortex damage data [16]; computational axon models [33,133]
what_is_missing: Routine effective-dose reporting [2]; frequency, duty cycle, current density and electrode size in the safety rule [18]; adjudication of excitation versus informational lesion [133]

drive_physically: Same pulses, delivered only while a subthalamic beta-band local field potential burst exceeds threshold [135]
proposed_primary_coupling: As open-loop DBS [33]; the biomarker gates delivery rather than altering coupling [135]
named_rival: Not established in this corpus; random intermittent stimulation did not match adaptive stimulation, so timing rather than intermittency carried the benefit [135]
dose_quantities_reported: Gating threshold plus the underlying pulse parameters; blinded motor scores improved 50%, about 27% better than continuous stimulation, with total stimulation time down 56% [135]
resolution_reported: Temporal resolution set by the burst detector; spatial as open-loop DBS [135]
dominant_evidence_base: Human, 8 patients with advanced Parkinson's disease, within-subject blinded comparison [135]
what_is_missing: What "dose" denotes when delivery is state-gated [135]; long-term controlled trials, not established in this corpus

invasiveness: Transcranial drive that deliberately induces a generalised seizure, with cognitive adverse effects as its limiting cost [263]
drive_physically: Charge-balanced current pulse trains through scalp electrodes, with placement, pulse amplitude, shape and width, and train frequency, directionality, polarity and duration as separate physical variables [261]
proposed_primary_coupling: Contested at the level of the drive itself: the antidepressant action is attributed to the induced seizure, to the electrical stimulation, or to their interaction, and the mechanism review that poses the question leaves it open [263]
named_rival: The seizure account against the direct-field account [263]; simulation puts ECT's suprathreshold volume well above that of magnetic seizure therapy, so comparable efficacy from a much more focal field favours the seizure [225,227]
dose_quantities_reported: Placement and pulse width are the decisive axes: ultrabrief 0.3 ms right unilateral gave 73% remission against 35% for ultrabrief bilateral in a 2 × 2 randomised design in 90 patients, so efficacy does not follow delivered charge [260]; total charge and energy are argued to be the wrong abstraction [261]; in macaque, seizure threshold was lowest near 16 pulses per second across 5–240 pulses per second and 230–565 mA [226]; three sessions weekly for three weeks [170], median six sessions to remission [171]
resolution_reported: Larger suprathreshold brain volume than MST in finite-element simulation of four ECT montages against three MST coils [225]; seizure induction immediate, course over weeks [260]
dominant_evidence_base: Human: meta-analysis in which real ECT beat simulated (sham) ECT and pharmacotherapy, with bilateral placement and higher dose better than unilateral and lower dose on efficacy [262]; randomised parameter trial, n = 90 [260]; two open-label head-to-heads against intravenous ketamine, response 41.2% versus 55.4% [170] and remission 63% versus 46% [171]; macaque threshold mapping [226]
what_is_missing: Whether the seizure or the field carries the effect [263]; a dosing abstraction better than charge or multiples of seizure threshold [261]; clinical frequencies sit far above the charge-minimising optimum measured in macaque [226]

invasiveness: Transcranial magnetic drive that deliberately induces a generalised seizure, with fewer cognitive adverse effects than ECT in a blinded head-to-head [227]
drive_physically: High-intensity, high-frequency magnetic pulse trains inducing an eddy current confined largely to superficial cortex [225]
proposed_primary_coupling: Seizure induction from a focal induced field, which reaches a smaller suprathreshold brain volume than any ECT montage at comparable clinical effect [225,227]
named_rival: As for ECT, the seizure against the field: comparable efficacy from a much more focal field is the main argument for the seizure account [227,263]
dose_quantities_reported: Coil design, train frequency and stimulator output: in macaque, thresholds were mapped across 5–100 pulses per second at 66–86% of maximum stimulator output, with the fewest pulses needed at mid-range frequencies [226]; field magnitude and suprathreshold volume from simulation [225]
resolution_reported: Field confined much more to superficial cortex than four ECT electrode configurations, in a finite-element comparison [225]; MST required more treatment sessions than ECT [227]
dominant_evidence_base: Human: one double-blind randomised trial at three hospitals in 73 adults — response 51.4% for MST against 42.1% for ultrabrief right unilateral ECT, sustained at six months, with significantly longer time to reorientation and fewer cognitive adverse effects [227]; macaque threshold mapping [226]; simulation [225]
what_is_missing: Which train parameters set the human seizure threshold [226]; any trial beyond the single blinded head-to-head [227]

invasiveness: Implanted extradural electrode; not established in this corpus as a therapy [30,31]
drive_physically: Not established in this corpus; the corpus's epidural material is recordings, not therapeutic drive [58]
proposed_primary_coupling: Indirect (I-wave) trans-synaptic activation of corticospinal neurons, with recruitment depending on current direction, measured as descending volleys [58]
resolution_reported: Millisecond ordering of direct and indirect descending volleys [58]; no spatial figure
dominant_evidence_base: Human epidural recordings, review [58]
what_is_missing: A therapeutic epidural cortical stimulation source of any kind [30,31]

drive_physically: Charge injection directly into grey matter through one or more electrodes of an array [248]
proposed_primary_coupling: Direct excitation of local neural elements, with axons before somata and current–distance relations setting the excited shell [34]; evoked percepts organised somatotopically by electrode [248]
named_rival: Not a labelled line: at one electrode, amplitude and frequency decide whether the percept is cutaneous or proprioceptive, and some electrodes are multimodal [249]
dose_quantities_reported: Amplitude grades perceived intensity [248]; detection thresholds fell from a median 31.5 µA at day 100 to 10.4 µA at day 1500 [250]; mean single-electrode phosphene threshold 66.8 ± 36.5 µA in visual cortex, falling substantially under simultaneous multi-electrode stimulation [251]; microelectrodes tolerate higher charge densities than the macroelectrode rule predicts [18]
resolution_reported: Single-electrode resolution, somatotopically ordered in somatosensory cortex [248] and one phosphene per electrode in visual cortex [251]; percepts stable over months [248], stimulation performance holding over 1,500 days [250]
dominant_evidence_base: Human: implanted participants with spinal cord injury [248,249,250] and a blind volunteer with a 96-channel occipital array for six months [251]; mammalian CNS review for the coupling account [34]
what_is_missing: Revised charge-density damage thresholds for chronic human microstimulation [18,250]; single-participant designs throughout [248,249,250,251]

family: TMS, single pulse and conventional rTMS
drive_physically: Pulsed magnetic field inducing an electric field in tissue; dose is every device parameter that shapes that field [9]
proposed_primary_coupling: Myelinated axon terminals of pyramidal cells and interneurons at the gyral crown, with spread through intracortical circuits and white matter (consensus, measured and modelled) [41]; modelling puts the lowest thresholds in intracortical axon terminals, with field magnitude mattering more than direction [57]
named_rival: Substantial somatosensory and auditory co-stimulation accompanies every pulse and must be controlled for [41]
dose_quantities_reported: Coil geometry, waveform, pulse parameters, train and session timing [9]; percentage of motor threshold as the clinical norm [15]; modelled E-field reported in 308 different ways [14]
resolution_reported: Simulated half-value depth 0.9–3.5 cm, with tangential spread 5 cm² for figure-8 and 34 cm² for circular coils, spherical head model [56]; current direction changes which interneuron circuits are recruited, read from epidural volleys [58]; the effective extent exceeds the induced field, since prefrontal rTMS reduced [<sup>11</sup>C]raclopride binding specifically in ipsilateral dorsal caudate in humans [143]
dominant_evidence_base: Human consensus plus measured epidural volleys [41,58]; computational thresholds [57]; expert safety guideline, seizure risk low at conventional parameters [42]
what_is_missing: An agreed E-field outcome measure [14]; a validated route from modelled field to physiology [15]

family: TMS, theta burst and accelerated protocols
drive_physically: Bursts of high-frequency pulses repeated at a theta rhythm [38]
proposed_primary_coupling: As single-pulse TMS, at axon terminals [41]; after-effects read as LTP/LTD-like plasticity [38]
named_rival: Which interneuron network a pulse recruits, indexed by anterior–posterior-current MEP latency, rather than plasticity capacity, explains responder status [59]
dose_quantities_reported: 20–190 s of stimulation; continuous versus intermittent pattern sets the direction of the excitability change [38]; a co-administered drug changes the delivered effect, with adjunctive D-cycloserine 100 mg over four weeks of iTBS giving a 6.15-point greater MADRS reduction (Hedges g = 0.99) and response 73.9% versus 29.3% in 50 patients [190]; accelerated protocols not established in this corpus
resolution_reported: After-effects outlasting stimulation and persisting beyond the ~30 min typical of earlier rTMS [38]
dominant_evidence_base: Human, healthy volunteers [38]; variability characterised in 56 adults [59]
what_is_missing: Reproducibility and responder rates of the after-effects are disputed [38,59]; any accelerated-protocol source

drive_physically: Sustained low-intensity current applied at the scalp [43]
proposed_primary_coupling: Compartment-specific membrane polarisation: about 0.12 mV per mV/mm at the soma along the somato-dendritic axis, largest at dendritic tips, with no clear threshold (rat hippocampal slice) [36]; morphology-dependent, layer V pyramidal cells most sensitive (rat, in vitro) [49]
named_rival: Fields too weak for direct effects: about 75% of scalp current is shunted, the minimum field affecting spiking is about 1 V/m in rat intracellular recordings, and 4–6 mA was needed to modulate human EEG alpha [50]
dose_quantities_reported: Up to 4 mA and 60 min/day, from more than 300,000 pooled sessions with no serious adverse events [43]; 2 mA at the scalp produced about 0.8 V/m measured in cortex in 10 patients [40]; about 0.5 mV/mm peak measured in superficial cortex [211]
resolution_reported: Polarisation time constants about 15–70 ms, with excitability changes outlasting the field by more than a second, rat slice [36]; field strength changed little with region or frequency in human and macaque recordings [211]; no focality figure in this corpus
dominant_evidence_base: Rat slice and in vitro [36,49]; human intracranial measurement [40,211]; pooled human safety data [43]
what_is_missing: Whether 1–2 mA modulates neurons directly [36,50]; a consensus in-tissue metric [14]

drive_physically: Sinusoidal current applied at the scalp [43]
proposed_primary_coupling: Spike-timing entrainment without rate change, dose-dependent at human-feasible intensities in awake macaque [51,52]; network resonance amplifies weak fields, largest when stimulation matches the intrinsic rhythm (ferret slice plus simulation) [37,53]
named_rival: Transcutaneous stimulation of peripheral nerves: anaesthetising the skin reduced tremor entrainment and peripheral stimulation alone reproduced the motor effects (rat and human) [54]; countered by entrainment persisting under topical anaesthesia in macaque [55]
dose_quantities_reported: Same envelope as tDCS, to 4 mA and 60 min/day [43]; frequency relative to the intrinsic rhythm [53]; endogenous fields for comparison were 2–4 mV/mm in ferret cortex [37]
resolution_reported: Phase locking altered without firing-rate change, including in macaque hippocampus and basal ganglia [51]; entrainment competes with ongoing oscillations and can reduce locking in strongly locked neurons [44]
dominant_evidence_base: Awake macaque single units [44,51,52]; ferret slice and simulation [37,53]; rat and human [54,55]
what_is_missing: Whether human effects at 1–2 mA are direct [50,54]; a state-dependent dose rule [44]

dose_quantities_reported: Only as part of a pooled tES safety envelope with tDCS and tACS: to 4 mA and 60 min/day, no serious adverse events over more than 300,000 sessions [43]
dominant_evidence_base: Human safety pooling only [43]
what_is_missing: Every mechanistic and dose-specific cell; absent from both comparison sources [30,31]

drive_physically: Two kHz carriers at slightly different frequencies whose overlap produces a low-frequency amplitude envelope [39]
proposed_primary_coupling: Envelope demodulation at the membrane: mouse neurons followed the envelope, hippocampal neurons were driven without driving overlying cortex, and motor responses were steered by current ratio [39]; in humans, modelled and cadaver-measured steering with changed hippocampal fMRI and improved episodic memory accuracy [45]
named_rival: Passive membrane filtering cannot extract the envelope; ion-channel rectification can, and predicts tonic firing or conduction block in superficial tissue at intensities that reach deep targets (computational) [60]; modelled suprathreshold TI needs about 75–230 V/m against about 0.1–1 V/m attainable in the human brain [48]; in macaque, TI altered spike timing but not rate and was about 80% less potent than tACS [46]
dose_quantities_reported: Carrier frequency, difference frequency, per-channel current and current ratio [39]; human studies mostly used 20 Hz or gamma-range envelopes [47]
resolution_reported: Steering claimed from models and cadaver measurements rather than from in vivo field recordings [45]; spike-timing effects without rate change in macaque [46]
dominant_evidence_base: Human systematic review: 48 records, 20 completed studies and 28 ongoing trials, 820 participants, well tolerated, evidence at Phase 1 level with efficacy untested [47]; mouse [39]; macaque [46]; computational [48,60]
what_is_missing: Efficacy of any kind [47]; adjudication of suprathreshold feasibility [46,48]; measured human in-brain envelope amplitude

drive_physically: Current pulses delivered to the cervical vagus [140]
proposed_primary_coupling: Recruitment of vagal afferents driving phasic locus coeruleus firing: rapid phasic bursts from 0.1 mA, with rate rising with current and pulse width, and pulse frequency shifting burst timing without changing total activity (rat) [140]
named_rival: Not established in this corpus for the implanted route
dose_quantities_reported: Current amplitude, pulse frequency, pulse width, train duration, inter-train interval [140]; effective dose often omitted in implantable practice [2]
resolution_reported: Half-second trains produce phasic bursts in rat locus coeruleus; trigeminal pulse-locked activity appears only above 1.2 mA, giving an amplitude window that separates the two [140]
dominant_evidence_base: Rat direct recordings across a parameter grid [140]; clinical use as standard care [31]
what_is_missing: Fibre-class selectivity: the vagus is a bundle of molecularly distinct afferent classes whose transduction is poorly established [157]; any human recording of the engaged pathway

drive_physically: Current pulses at the auricular branch of the vagus [146]
proposed_primary_coupling: Assumed to be the same afferent recruitment as cervical VNS [140]; in humans indexed only by proxies [146]
named_rival: Null engagement: pooled continuous stimulation gives strong evidence for no pupil effect (g = 0.002, BF01 = 21.9) while pulsed stimulation gives strong evidence for one (g = 0.36, BF10 = 50.8) [146]
dose_quantities_reported: Amplitude, pulse width, frequency, and pulsed versus continuous delivery as the decisive parameter [146]
resolution_reported: Not established in this corpus; the human read-out is a pupil proxy rather than a spatial or temporal measurement [146]
dominant_evidence_base: Human living Bayesian meta-analysis, 18 studies, N = 771 [146]; rat parametric work by extension [140]
what_is_missing: A direct human measure of target engagement; separation of vagal from trigeminal recruitment at the ear [140,157]

dose_quantities_reported: Appears only as a recruitment control during VNS, where pulse-locked trigeminal activity appeared above 1.2 mA in rat [140]
dominant_evidence_base: Rat, as a control condition in a VNS parameter study [140]
what_is_missing: Any source treating the trigeminal nerve as the intended target; it appears in neither cross-modality comparison source [30,31]

invasiveness: Implanted nerve cuff with a respiration sensor; serious adverse events in under 2% [252]
drive_physically: Current pulses to the hypoglossal nerve, gated to inspiration, producing timed tongue-protrusor contraction [252]
proposed_primary_coupling: Excitation of a somatic motor nerve, with a mechanical endpoint (airway patency) rather than a modulated state [252]
dose_quantities_reported: Pulse width 90 against 120 µs and frequency 33 against 40 Hz, amplitude in volts, therapeutic window counted in tolerable voltage steps; the longer, faster configuration lowered the amplitude needed for functional protrusion across all three electrode configurations without changing the usable window [253]
resolution_reported: Stimulation gated to the respiratory cycle, so the temporal unit is the breath [252]; no spatial figure in this corpus
dominant_evidence_base: Human: 126 CPAP-intolerant patients, median apnoea–hypopnoea index down 68% from 29.3 to 9.0 events/hour at 12 months, with a randomised therapy-withdrawal substudy confirming device dependence [252]; pooled analysis of 30 studies (549 patients across 26 single-arm studies, 273 across 4 randomised trials), index down 20.11 events/hour (95% CI 23.13 to 17.10) at one year and 15.60 beyond [254]
what_is_missing: Randomised evidence: only 4 of the 30 pooled studies were randomised [254]

drive_physically: Current pulses to the occipital nerves, producing paraesthesia in the stimulated field [255]
named_rival: Not established in this corpus; a 30% intensity arm matched the 100% arm, so a dose-dependent therapeutic effect cannot be separated from a non-specific one [255]
dose_quantities_reported: Intensity expressed as a percentage of the individually determined paraesthesia-to-near-discomfort range rather than in mA, set at 100% or 30% [255]
dominant_evidence_base: Human: randomised, double-blind, multicentre phase 3 dose-controlled trial in medically intractable chronic cluster headache, median weekly attack frequency falling substantially by weeks 21–24 (p < 0.0001), similarly in both arms [255]
what_is_missing: A sham comparison, which an unmistakable paraesthesia makes impossible, and with it the mechanism of benefit [255]

drive_physically: Current pulses in the epidural space over the spinal cord [2]
proposed_primary_coupling: Recruitment of large myelinated dorsal-root afferents rather than motoneurons or interneurons directly, which then engage motor pools trans-synaptically; modelled and confirmed in rats for intensity and electrode position [61]
dose_quantities_reported: Amplitude, pulse width, frequency, waveform; classification proposed by target plus waveform and dose, with effective dose often omitted [2]; charge-density and charge-per-phase limit by inheritance [17]
resolution_reported: Recruitment order and threshold as a function of electrode position, modelled and rat-validated [61]; kHz waveforms optimised to inactivate sodium channels from the closed state can block conduction without an onset burst (computational) [62]
dominant_evidence_base: Computational model with rat validation [61,62]; expert consensus taxonomy [2]; clinical use [31]
what_is_missing: Human mechanism data; frequency and duty-cycle terms in the safety rule [18]

family: Peripheral nerve stimulation and functional electrical stimulation
invasiveness: Surface electrodes through to fully implanted systems [245]
drive_physically: Charge-balanced current pulses to intact peripheral motor nerves, with the safety envelope set by charge-injection limits rather than by seizure or cognitive risk [245]
proposed_primary_coupling: Excitation of peripheral motor axons, with contraction graded by amplitude, pulse width and frequency [245]
named_rival: Recruitment is non-selective, spatially fixed and temporally synchronous rather than following the size principle, and the textbook strict reverse (large-to-small) order is not supported; synchronous firing of the same units is the source of the rapid fatigue [246]
dose_quantities_reported: Amplitude, pulse width and frequency modulation as the grading variables [245]; the same peripheral drive alone reproduced tACS motor effects in rats and humans [54]; kHz waveforms optimised to inactivate sodium channels from the closed state block conduction without an onset burst (computational) [62]
resolution_reported: Spatially fixed recruitment, so the stimulated population does not rotate as in voluntary contraction [246]; the outcome is a graded mechanical action rather than a modulated state [245]
dominant_evidence_base: Human: meta-analysis of 18 randomised trials after stroke, moderate pooled effect on activity driven mainly by upper-limb function with smaller gains in walking speed [247]; family review across upper and lower extremity, bladder, bowel and respiratory neuroprostheses [245]
what_is_missing: A selective recruitment method that reproduces the size principle, and fatigue-resistant parameter sets [246]

drive_physically: Focused pressure wave, pulsed, delivered through the skull [20]
proposed_primary_coupling: Contested, with at least four candidates: intramembrane cavitation rectified into capacitance change (computational) [65]; mechanosensitive channels — TREK-1, TREK-2, TRAAK and NaV1.5 currents modulated by up to about 23% at 10 MHz and 0.3–4.9 W/cm² in oocytes [67], Piezo1 required in vivo in mouse cortex [68], astrocytic TRPA1 driving Best1 glutamate release onto neuronal NMDA receptors [69], and CFTR chloride flow at 0.8 MHz and 0.20 MPa in HEK cells [70]; acoustic radiation force, with responses growing from 0.5 to 43 MHz, which excludes cavitation in salamander retina [66]; and heating, where suppression tracked temperature and was independent of duty cycle, peak pressure and modulation frequency in rat thalamus [71]
named_rival: Peripheral confound rather than direct coupling: guinea-pig activation was abolished by auditory-nerve transection or cochlear fluid removal [74], mouse cortical patterns matched the auditory pathway [75], and in humans the standard motor inhibition was driven by auditory stimulation across four experiments [77]; countered by intact motor responses in genetically deaf mice once pulse edges were smoothed [76]; scalp somatosensory sensation is a further route, driven by particle displacement [78]
dose_quantities_reported: Six reporting domains: transducer and drive system, drive settings, free-field acoustic parameters, pulse timing, in situ exposure estimates and intensity parameters [20]; mechanical index at or below 1.9 as non-significant risk plus three alternative thermal criteria, by the authors' statement expert opinion and not safety limits [19]; across 32 studies and 37 experiments, duty cycle (p = 0.046) and sonication duration (p = 0.04) predicted direction of effect while I<sub>SPPA</sub> alone did not (p = 0.256) [79]
resolution_reported: Not established in this corpus as a measured human focal volume; in situ exposure is estimated rather than measured [20]; response duration tracked pulse duration in mouse [76]
dominant_evidence_base: Human systematic review and meta-analysis, self-declared provisional [79]; human experiments [77,78]; rodent [68,71,74,75,76]; in vitro [66,67,70]; computational [65]
what_is_missing: Which parameter sets the direction of effect [71,79]; complete parameter reporting [79]; the threshold for significant risk [19]

invasiveness: Transcranial but tissue-destructive: an irreversible lesion without an incision [86]
drive_physically: High-intensity focused ultrasound absorbed as heat at the focus [85]
proposed_primary_coupling: Thermal coagulation, with dose expressed as cumulative equivalent minutes at 43 °C [85]
named_rival: Not established in this corpus; the same physical modality is reversible at low intensity, so thermal dose rather than modality decides [85,86]
dose_quantities_reported: Temperature and thermal dose [85]; achievable peak temperature limited by skull density ratio (positive, p = 0.009) and skull volume (negative, p = 0.023) in 25 patients [87]
resolution_reported: Lesion placed accurately enough to beat a sham procedure [86]; no millimetre figure in this corpus; effect is immediate and permanent [86]
dominant_evidence_base: Human randomised sham-controlled trial: hand tremor 18.1 to 9.6 at three months versus 16.0 to 15.8 with sham, gait disturbance in 36% and paraesthesia or numbness in 38% [86]; human retrospective series [87]
what_is_missing: A per-patient account of skull transmission [87]; comparison against DBS on the same endpoints [31]

drive_physically: Low-pressure focused ultrasound driving oscillation of circulating microbubbles at the vessel wall [80]
proposed_primary_coupling: Microbubble cavitation at the endothelium rather than absorption in tissue, which is why it works far below ablative intensity [80]
named_rival: Sterile inflammation as an intrinsic consequence: damage-associated molecular patterns and a parenchymal inflammatory response lasting about 24 h, compared by the authors to ischaemia or mild traumatic brain injury (rat) [83]; against microbubble dose as the controlling variable, with no significant NF-κB change at clinical imaging doses and oedema, degeneration and microhaemorrhage at high doses (rat) [84]
dose_quantities_reported: Temporal peak acoustic power 0.2–11.5 W in rabbit [80]; 0.28 ± 0.05 MPa mean peak pressure at 551.5 kHz, 10 ms bursts, 2 Hz PRF, held at a fraction of the ultraharmonic-emission threshold, with opening and no detectable damage at 50% scaling [81]; microbubble dose [84]
resolution_reported: Opening confined to the targeted volume and imageable by contrast-enhanced MR, reversible and repeatable [80,82]; enhancement scaled linearly with the chosen pressure fraction [81]
dominant_evidence_base: Rabbit [80] and rat [81,83,84]; human phase I in five patients with Alzheimer's disease, safe and reversible with no group-level amyloid change [82]
what_is_missing: Therapeutic benefit as distinct from barrier opening [82]; an agreed inflammatory threshold [83,84]

invasiveness: Non-invasive and neuronavigated, with high tolerability and no serious adverse events reported [228]
drive_physically: Single ultrashort ultrasound shockwave pulses of roughly 3 µs rather than a continuous or tone-burst beam, so the drive has essentially no duty cycle [228]
proposed_primary_coupling: Not established in this corpus: the introductory paper lists candidates — transient membrane pore formation, neurotransmitter and neurotrophin changes, microglial activation, nitric oxide signalling — without establishing one [228]; in mice, clinical-range energy produced calcium influx, raised c-Fos in dentate gyrus and transiently reorganised limbic network connectivity, reverting within about ten minutes [230]
named_rival: A second mechanism appears at a modest energy increase: 0.25 mJ/mm² triggered spreading depolarisation waves where 0.05 mJ/mm² produced the direct activation pattern (mouse) [230]
dose_quantities_reported: Energy flux density 0.2–0.3 mJ/mm², about 3 µs per pulse, 5 Hz, about 6,000 pulses per session, with measured temporal-peak intensity falling roughly 80–90% through human skull [228]; the randomised trial used 6,000 pulses at 0.20 mJ/mm² and 5 Hz [229]
resolution_reported: Neuronavigated focal delivery [228]; mouse network changes reverting to baseline within about ten minutes [230]; no measured human focal volume
dominant_evidence_base: Human: the sham-controlled primary endpoint was negative — in a double-blind crossover trial in 60 patients on standard therapy, CERAD corrected total score rose 2.22 points after verum against 1.00 after sham at three months, but the condition-by-session interaction was not significant (P = .68), with benefit only in a prespecified subgroup aged 70 or under and successful blinding [229]; the 35-patient open-label series it supersedes reported three-month improvement correlated with memory-network connectivity [228]; mouse imaging [230]
what_is_missing: A confirmed clinical effect, since the sham-controlled trial does not reproduce the open-label result [228,229]; an established coupling mechanism [228,230]

invasiveness: Fully non-invasive, with no adverse clinical or laboratory effects in the first human study [256,259]
drive_physically: Focused ultrasound aimed at a sub-organ visceral target — splenic, hepatic or hepatoportal — rather than at a nerve trunk or the brain [256]
proposed_primary_coupling: Mechanical activation of nerve terminals inside the organ with afferent relay to brain: splenic stimulation engaged the cholinergic anti-inflammatory pathway comparably with surgical VNS and hepatic stimulation altered glucose regulation, with imaging showing engagement of metabolism-related brain regions [256]; the hepatoportal effect required an intact liver-to-brain pathway, verified by denervation, in mice, rats and swine [258]
named_rival: A local tissue effect rather than a neural reflex [256]; in humans the effect did not differ by stimulation mode or across a roughly fifteen-fold intensity difference, which is hard to reconcile with a dose-dependent mechanical-neural mechanism [259]
dose_quantities_reported: Human: three minutes delivered in intermittent 15 s intervals, either swept continuously at 11.7 mW/cm² or focused-pulsed at 174.8–225.4 mW/cm² [259]; in mice the benefit depended on specific stimulation parameters [257]
resolution_reported: Sub-organ targeting rather than focality in neural tissue [256]; in humans, ex vivo TNF production fell for more than two hours and returned to baseline by 24 h [259]
dominant_evidence_base: Human first-in-human study in healthy volunteers [259]; rodent work from two independent groups [256,257], with single-cell RNA sequencing implicating T and B cell populations [257]; cross-species to swine [258]
what_is_missing: Any human measurement of the neurotransmitter relay, which remains inferred from the preclinical work, and any energy–response relationship [259]

drive_physically: Red to near-infrared light applied at the scalp, for example an 810 nm LED helmet or a 905 nm laser [22]
proposed_primary_coupling: Cytochrome c oxidase as photoacceptor, argued from competition with potassium cyanide and from efficacy tracking the enzyme's absorption spectrum, with 670 and 830 nm effective and 728 nm not; cell death fell from 83.6% to 43.5% at 300 µM KCN in primary neurons [88]; nitric oxide photodissociation as the signalling step [89]
named_rival: Insufficient delivered dose: more than 99% of light absorbed or scattered by human skull, maximum transmittance 0.31% for a 905 nm laser and 0.71% for an 810 nm LED helmet, with mitochondrial responses appearing only 14–775 times above the transmitted level [22]; against Monte Carlo simulation putting up to about 15% of incident energy at cortex transcranially and about 1% intranasally, reduced by melanin [23]
dose_quantities_reported: Wavelength, irradiance in mW/cm², fluence in J/cm², with a claimed biphasic dose response in which low fluence stimulates more than high [21]
resolution_reported: Deposition concentrated in ventromedial prefrontal cortex in simulation [23]; no measured focal volume or time constant in this corpus
dominant_evidence_base: In vitro primary neurons and HeLa cells [88,89]; human skull specimens with in vitro dose comparison [22]; photon-transport simulation [23]; proponent review [21]
what_is_missing: Agreement on the fraction of light reaching cortex [22,23]; skin pigmentation as a reported covariate [23]; any dose standard [21]

drive_physically: A molecule delivered to plasma and distributed by blood flow and barrier transport [164]
proposed_primary_coupling: Ligand binding at a receptor, described by affinity, occupancy and efficacy in the operational model [91], with exposure at the target site, target binding and expression of pharmacological activity as the three steps that have to be shown separately [24]; for neurosteroids, positive allosteric modulation of GABA-A rather than agonism [179]
named_rival: The coupling step can be membrane-biophysical rather than a lock-and-key receptor event, with anaesthetic-sensitive sites in ordered lipid domains [184]; and receptor location can decide the effect, since psychedelic plasticity requires intracellular rather than surface 5-HT2A receptors [92]
dose_quantities_reported: Ketamine 0.5 mg/kg as a single infusion, with improvement at 110 min, response 71% and remission 29% at day 1 (n = 18, crossover) [166]; brexanolone as a single 60 h titrated infusion, Hamilton reduction 14.6 versus 12.1 points at 60 h [180]; occupancy as a dose proxy, 38–87% D2 predicting response with thresholds near 65% for response, 72% for extrapyramidal symptoms and 78% for hyperprolactinaemia [26], and windows of 65–80% D2 and 70–80% SERT [27]; plasma exposure as AUC and C<sub>max</sub> [25]
resolution_reported: Spatial selectivity comes from receptor distribution and barrier transport, not from delivery [164]; temporal profile is pharmacokinetic, and the ketamine effect outlasted clearance by about a week [166]
dominant_evidence_base: Human randomised trials [166,180]; human PET [26,27]; systematic review of 110 studies and 37,193 participants [28]
what_is_missing: Measured target-site concentration rather than modelled [164]; an efficacy term alongside occupancy, since partial agonists keep extrapyramidal risk low at high occupancy [28]

drive_physically: A molecule absorbed from the gut into plasma [186]
proposed_primary_coupling: As intravenous: receptor binding and occupancy [91]
named_rival: As intravenous [184,92]
dose_quantities_reported: Zuranolone 50 mg once daily for 14 days, Hamilton-17 least-squares mean difference −4.0 (95% CI −6.3 to −1.7), n = 196 [181]; levodopa dosing complicated by erratic plasma uptake and large dose-to-dose variability [186]
resolution_reported: Temporal profile imposed by absorption: pulsatile versus continuous exposure of the same receptors gives different long-term outcomes [186]; no spatial selectivity beyond receptor distribution [164]
dominant_evidence_base: Human phase 3 trial [181]; clinical pharmacology review [186]
what_is_missing: Delivery consistency rather than receptor pharmacology as the limiting factor [186]; whether these agents outperform existing treatments, judged insufficient by one review [181]

drive_physically: A molecule deposited on nasal mucosa [161]
proposed_primary_coupling: Direct nose-to-brain transport along olfactory and trigeminal pathways by perineural and perivascular bulk flow [161]
named_rival: Systemic absorption rather than direct transport; the pharmacokinetic evidence for a direct human route is contested [161]
dose_quantities_reported: Flexibly dosed intranasal esketamine added to a newly started oral antidepressant, n = 227, greater MADRS improvement by day 28, with dissociation, nausea, vertigo, dysgeusia and dizziness generally resolving within about 1.5 h [169]
resolution_reported: Simulation of intranasal light puts about 1% of energy at cortex, which is the nearest analogue in this corpus rather than a drug measurement [23]; no measured human nose-to-brain distribution
dominant_evidence_base: Human phase 3 registration trial [169]; mechanism review, mixed species [161]
what_is_missing: Quantification of the direct fraction in humans [161]; blinding, since dissociative effects are unmasking [169]

drive_physically: A gas taken up across the alveolar membrane [185]
proposed_primary_coupling: Anaesthetic action at sites inside ion channels and within the plasma membrane [184]
dose_quantities_reported: Nitrous oxide, one-hour inhalations at 25% or 50%, n = 24 crossover: improvement versus placebo (P = 0.01), no difference between concentrations (P = 0.58), adverse events far fewer at 25% (P < 0.001) [185]
resolution_reported: Separation from placebo emerged at weeks 1 and 2 rather than at 2 or 24 hours, so the outcome outlasts exposure by weeks [185]; no spatial selectivity reported
dominant_evidence_base: Human phase 2 crossover trial [185]; in vitro mechanism review [184]
what_is_missing: Dose–response for efficacy, which saturated while side effects remained dose-dependent [185]

drive_physically: A molecule infused into the cerebrospinal fluid compartment [163]
proposed_primary_coupling: Receptor occupancy placed at the spinal cord rather than the brain: GABA-B agonism where the circuit is, not where the side effects are [163]
dose_quantities_reported: Continuous pump infusion of baclofen: tone fell in all 20 patients and spasms were reduced in 18 of 19, maintained over a mean 19.2 months, in patients who had failed the oral route [163]
resolution_reported: Compartment-level rather than focal selectivity; continuous rather than pulsed delivery [163]
dominant_evidence_base: Human randomised double-blind crossover trial, n = 20 [163]
what_is_missing: Target-site concentration measurement [164]; comparison with implanted stimulation on the same endpoint [2]

drive_physically: A sustained pressure gradient driving bulk flow of infusate through the extracellular space [160]
proposed_primary_coupling: Convective transport replacing diffusion, so distribution is set by infusion physics rather than by molecular diffusivity [160]
dose_quantities_reported: Infusion rate, volume, catheter placement and tissue hydraulic conductivity; distribution-to-infusion volume about 6:1 for ¹¹¹In-transferrin and about 13:1 for ¹⁴C-sucrose, with local concentrations orders of magnitude above achievable systemic levels [160]
resolution_reported: Centimetres of spread rather than millimetres, with the large molecule more uniformly distributed at 24 h [160]
dominant_evidence_base: Mixed-species intraparenchymal infusion experiments [160]
what_is_missing: Human outcome data in this corpus; comparison with FUS barrier opening as the other route for large molecules [80,160]

invasiveness: Non-invasive and home-delivered, with adherence of 85–90% and no serious treatment-related adverse events over six months [234]
drive_physically: Patterned light and sound delivered to the sense organs at a chosen frequency [231]
proposed_primary_coupling: Sensory transduction into a rhythmic cortical response whose amplitude is resonant rather than flat: human EEG stepped across 1–100 Hz flicker showed peaks near 10, 20, 40 and 80 Hz [231]
named_rival: Linear superposition rather than entrainment: steady-state responses were reproduced by shifting and summing rate-matched transient evoked responses, with no signature of oscillatory entrainment at the stimulation frequency (human) [232]
dose_quantities_reported: Frequency as the dose axis, with measured resonance peaks [231]; 40 Hz combined light and sound, one hour daily for three months [233]; EEG-verified 40 Hz audio-visual delivery over six months [234]
resolution_reported: Frequency specificity in the driven response [231]; delivery is whole-pathway rather than focal, since selectivity comes from the sense organ and not from a field [231,232]
dominant_evidence_base: Human: the largest sham-controlled trial missed its primary cognitive composite in 70 analysable patients with mild-to-moderate Alzheimer's disease randomised 2:1, with nominally favourable unadjusted secondaries — MMSE decline reduced 76%, ADCS-ADL decline 77%, whole-brain volume loss 69% [234]; pilot work showed tolerability and reliable EEG entrainment, and in 15 patients less ventricular dilation and hippocampal atrophy [233]; human EEG mechanism studies [231,232]
what_is_missing: Whether the driven response involves an entrained oscillator at all [231,232]; a positive primary endpoint [234]; multiplicity-adjusted secondary outcomes [234]

invasiveness: Non-invasive transmastoid electrodes, described as simple and safe [235]
drive_physically: Direct or alternating current passed between mastoid electrodes into the vestibular periphery [235]
proposed_primary_coupling: DC bias of firing in vestibular primary afferents at the spike-initiation zone rather than at the hair cell or the central nuclei, with irregular afferents most sensitive; the vector of biased signals converging in the vestibular nuclei predicts the direction and size of body sway across montages [235]
dose_quantities_reported: Current amplitude 0.1–4 mA, session duration 12 s to 24 h, and direct, sinusoidal or stochastic waveforms, extracted from 53 clinical trials, some parameters near-standard within an indication and others with no convention [237]
resolution_reported: Organ-level selectivity set by montage and polarity rather than by focality of the field [235]; evokes eye movements and postural responses without head motion, so vestibular processing can be dissociated from actual acceleration [236]
dominant_evidence_base: Human: review-level forward model from montage to sway [235]; systematic parameter review across 53 clinical trials in vestibular loss, cerebellar ataxia, Parkinson's disease, post-stroke neglect, motion sickness and balance impairment [237]; cross-species mechanism review [236]
what_is_missing: Parameter consensus across indications, and pooled efficacy estimates by indication [237]

drive_physically: A constant magnetic field held over the scalp, with no time variation and therefore no induced electric field [238]
proposed_primary_coupling: Not established in this corpus: no accepted transduction pathway exists for a static field, and the reported excitability change was localised to intracortical rather than peripheral or spinal mechanisms by control conditions [238]
named_rival: Non-replication: ten minutes at matched magnet geometry produced no MEP modulation in 18 subjects, with or without a concurrent attentional task [240]
dose_quantities_reported: Flux density at cortex, about 160–170 mT at 2 cm from the scalp for a 45 × 30 mm N45 magnet and about 160–245 mT for N52 magnets, with protocols of 5–15 min, 20–30 min or two hours, up to three daily sessions [241]
resolution_reported: Focality set by magnet geometry, with effects reported as site-dependent across motor, somatosensory and visual cortex, cerebellum and spinal cord [239]; after-effects outlasting a ten-minute application by several minutes [238]
dominant_evidence_base: Human: single-session excitability studies, with MEP amplitude reduced by up to about 25% after ten minutes [238]; qualitative pooling of 27 studies, predominantly inhibitory, with no aggregated effect sizes [239]; four randomised clinical trials, including 50 patients with levodopa-induced dyskinesia and a phase 2 ALS trial with no short-term functional difference but a 73% lower risk of death or tracheostomy at 18 months [241]
what_is_missing: A pooled effect-size estimate, so the effect size rests on single studies [239]; replication of the excitability effect [238,240]; any transduction mechanism [238]

invasiveness: Implanted or intraoperative surface device; cooling produced no appreciable cortical damage even at low temperatures [242]
drive_physically: Heat extraction from tissue, delivered in preclinical work by thermoelectric (Peltier) devices [242]
proposed_primary_coupling: Temperature dependence of channel kinetics and synaptic release, so the drive slows every temperature-dependent conductance and release step at once [242]
dose_quantities_reported: Target temperature: about 20 °C terminates paroxysmal activity in vitro and below 24 °C aborts seizures within seconds in vivo [242]; cooling a songbird premotor nucleus slowed song by up to 45% while leaving acoustic structure intact, graded with temperature [244]; achieved human cortical cooling was only about 0.6–2 °C at 10–15 mm depth [243]
resolution_reported: Region-specific and graded, present only while cooled: cooling one nucleus changed behavioural tempo while cooling the downstream nucleus did not [244]; thermal penetration limited to the first 10–15 mm from the human cortical surface [243]
dominant_evidence_base: Preclinical: in vitro and in vivo seizure work, reviewed [242]; songbird causal manipulation [244]; human and canine intraoperative thermometry [243]
what_is_missing: The gap between species: the 20–24 °C that works preclinically [242] cannot currently be delivered at depth in human cortex, where surface cooling achieved 0.6–2 °C [243]; any human therapeutic series

invasiveness: Implanted penetrating arrays in participants who also carry recording arrays [250]
drive_physically: Charge injection through array electrodes used as an input channel alongside neural recording [248]
proposed_primary_coupling: Direct cortical excitation writing contact location and pressure information into somatosensory cortex for closed-loop prosthetic control [248]
dose_quantities_reported: Per-electrode amplitude, with detection thresholds of a median 31.5 µA at day 100 falling to 10.4 µA at day 1500 [250]; amplitude and frequency set the modality of the percept as well as its magnitude [249]
resolution_reported: Single-electrode write-in, with percepts stable over months [248]; stimulated arrays retained signal amplitude better than unstimulated ones over 1,500 days [250]
dominant_evidence_base: Human: single-participant implanted series [248,249,250] and a six-month 96-channel visual cortex implant [251]; the corpus's other closed-loop exemplars gate a fixed drive on a measured signal rather than writing in — biomarker-gated DBS [135] and cavitation-feedback ultrasound [81]
what_is_missing: Performance of a full decode-and-write-in loop as a system, and any multi-participant series [248,250]
